transcript:
Meeting header: Rate Shaping & KV Cache Pilot Checkpoint
Date/Time: 2026-06-11 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Omar Haddad (CTO, PolarWave), Dana Lee (Head of MLOps), Priya Menon (SRE)

Summary: quick sync to review last week's throughput runs, surface a surprising cold-start penalty, discuss rate-shaping approach vs rigid concurrency limits, and agree next steps for a controlled sweep and data handoff.

Topics: throughput numbers, continuous batching behavior, KV cache warmup/evictions, queueing/backpressure, burst capacity, cost delta for reserved slots.

[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Maya from Redwood, Ethan's with me on the runbook. how's PolarWave doing?
[00:08] Omar: good, thanks. busy week, but this pilot's been helpful. we saw the dropoff you warned about on long sequences though.
[00:14] Ethan: yeah, quick context - last run we pushed a pattern that imitates your weekend bulk ingestion, high concurrency spikes followed by long-tail completion. we saw steady throughput but a p99 that regressed when a lot of cold KV cache misses happened.
[00:29] Dana: i can confirm, our users saw some slower responses during the ramp on Saturday. felt like queue saturation? maybe the queue depth spiked and then a bunch of tokens got serialized.
[00:40] Priya: and there were a couple of 503s in our logs right when the spike hit. not many but we care about the spikes.
[00:46] Ethan: important note: the backend we ran this on was a mix of dedicated and burst fallback, so when the primary pool reached saturation it routed to the fallback model variant which has slightly different tokenization, that also adds noise to latencies.
[01:02] Omar: mmh, can we avoid the fallback? we need more consistent outputs for that endpoint.
[01:06] Maya: yes, the options are: increase reserved capacity for predictable throughput, or adjust rate-shaping client-side so we avoid hitting the pool threshold. also we can tune continuous batching windows and KV cache warmup to reduce cold miss frequency.
[01:20] Dana: what's Redwood's recommendation here? we are cost-sensitive but consistency for the pipeline is higher priority for this stage of the pilot.
[01:28] Ethan: for cost-conscious + consistent latency: implement a token-bucket rate shaper at the API gateway that targets about 70-80% of observed per-GPU concurrency. that reduces queue tail events. then tune the continuous batcher to a slightly longer max-wait (30ms -> 50ms) to increase batch sizes during ramps. that increases throughput efficiency and reduces per-token cost.
[01:49] Priya: increasing wait to 50ms — will that hurt tail latency for low concurrency periods?
[01:54] Ethan: small impact, but we can have adaptive windows: short wait when concurrency is low, expand when the system detects ramping. Redwood runtime exposes an endpoint with per-route heuristics for that.
[02:06] Omar: can you say more about the KV cache behavior? the cold-start penalty looked big.
[02:11] Ethan: sure — we observed cold KV cache miss rate of ~22% at the start of a spike. two things: your workload uses few repeated prefixes per session so the cache needs warmup, and our eviction LRU parameters were default for that fleet. we can change the working set size and pin a small hot-slab for the most common prefixes.
[02:30] Maya: to be clear we can pin the top N prefixes for PolarWave as a cache static region, that helps the first 1–2 seconds of the spike. there's a tradeoff in memory vs hit-rate.
[02:39] Dana: sounds promising. what's the memory hit look like?
[02:42] Ethan: small for a handful of prefixes — maybe a few hundred MB. if you want to pin more we can quantify the delta. also we noticed some mis-tagging in our telemetry that labeled a few sessions under the wrong model variant, that contributed to apparent instability.
[02:57] Priya: ok, telemetry cleanup is on us, we'll send a corrected trace.
[03:00] [03:00] Maya: perfect. next — on queueing/backpressure we tested two approaches: conservative concurrency caps vs rate shaping. concurrency caps were simple but caused drop in throughput at mid-ramp; rate shaping smoothed demand and kept throughput higher but required client-side changes.
[03:19] Omar: so which do you recommend for our roadmap? short term we can change client — long term we'd like reserved capacity.
[03:27] Ethan: short term: rate shaping with a token-bucket + adaptive batching. medium term: reserve a small dedicated pool for the endpoint (1–2 GPUs depending on load) to guarantee tail SLOs. Reserved is the only way to avoid fallback routing entirely.
[03:43] Dana: what's the pricing gap for a small reserved pool vs pure burst?
[03:47] Maya: I'll send the delta spreadsheet after the call — quick estimate is roughly 20–35% higher per-hour but it flattens cost per token because you avoid fallback inefficiencies. I'll include burst vs reserved cost projections with your traffic curve.
[04:00] Omar: thanks. another oddity — we saw a bunch of responses with slightly different formatting when fallback kicked in (some tokenization differences). that caused a downstream parser to fail in a few cases. can Redwood force same tokenizer across variants?
[04:13] Ethan: not always — model family differences can change tokenization. but we can enforce a pre-tokenization step on the client or use a pinned model variant in the reserved pool to keep consistency. we also can run a quick sanitization step in the response pipeline to avoid breaking your parser.
[04:28] Priya: i like the pre-tokenization idea, less brittle.
[04:31] Maya: ok noted.
[04:33] [04:33] Ethan: quick note about the p99 buckets — we instrumented per-route p50/p95/p99 and also split p99 into 99 and 99.9. your p99.9 was the outlier in the Saturday test, correlates with cache cold misses and a tiny number of goroutine stalls during the fallback routing.
[04:51] Dana: goroutine stalls? do you mean the runtime thread pool had backpressure?
[04:55] Ethan: yeah, the runtime uses a small thread pool for async IO and a lock in one path caused a micro pause — we've got a patch in canary that reduces lock contention on large fan-in. we'll run it for a short window to confirm it's safe.
[05:08] Omar: can we include that canary in the next run?
[05:11] Ethan: yes — I can deploy canary to a subset of your requests or run a private run for the topology used in your trace.
[05:18] Maya: on telemetry sharing — Omar, you mentioned sending the 72-hour trace. please scrub PII and send the S3 link to the shared folder. we'll ingest and run the replay through Redwood's profiling harness.
[05:29] Omar: yep, we'll do that.
[05:31] Priya: about the controlled sweep — what parameters do you need?
[05:34] Ethan: ideally: concurrency targets (4,6,8), request size distribution, sequence length distribution, and a weekend-like burst pattern (90th percentile spike factor). also mark whether you want fallback allowed.
[05:46] Dana: we'll provide concurrency and sequence length histograms.
[05:49] [05:49] Maya: timeline — Ethan, can you run the controlled sweep and post results by next Thurs (2026-06-18)?
[05:55] Ethan: yes, I'll run three runs: baseline (current params), rate-shaper + adaptive batching, and reserved small pool + tuned KV slab. I'll add the canary patch as a fourth quick run if stability looks ok.
[06:07] Omar: what metrics will you surface? p50/p95/p99/p99.9, CPU/GPU utilization, KV hit rate, average batch size, and cost per 1M tokens.
[06:17] Ethan: correct. I'll also report queue depth time-series and cold miss timeline so you can see where headroom forms.
[06:24] Priya: for the cost numbers, can you include the delta for enabling a pinned hot-slab vs not? that helps our infra budget.
[06:30] Ethan: yes, slab memory delta and cost impact will be included.
[06:33] [06:33] Dana: any security or compliance blockers with the dedicated pool? we need to confirm KMS integration and audit logs.
[06:40] Maya: no blockers — Redwood Private and Dedicated both integrate with enterprise KMS and provide per-request audit logs. I will attach SOC2 and data residency notes with the pricing email.
[06:50] Omar: perfect. 
[06:52] Priya: a question on throttling — if we implement the token-bucket rate-shaper client-side, what happens if a client ignores it? does Redwood enforce a server-side fallback?
[06:59] Ethan: Redwood enforces per-customer global rate limits and will apply request rejection or backpressure headers. we can also set soft limits with 429+Retry-After which is friendlier. but ultimately, if a client ignores limits, the system will return 429s for excess requests.
[07:15] Dana: ok. do you have sample client code for token-bucket shaping?
[07:19] Maya: yes — I'll share a small Node/Python snippet in the shared folder.
[07:23] [07:23] Omar: another operational ask: can Redwood expose a hook for us to pre-warm the KV cache during scheduled spikes? a cron job to ping with common prefixes?
[07:32] Ethan: absolutely — we can run a warmup function or provide a pre-warm API call pattern. we'll document recommended warmup sequences so you don't pay for unnecessary tokens.
[07:43] Priya: great. that would help.
[07:45] Maya: to recap next steps: Ethan will run the sweep and post results; Maya will send pricing and compliance docs; PolarWave will send 72h trace and histograms; implement client-side rate shaping snippet. any other items?
[07:59] Omar: just one more — can we get a short runbook for incident response if we hit tail SLO breaches during ramp?
[08:06] Maya: yes, we'll draft a 1-page runbook with immediate mitigation steps (apply rate-shaper, shift to reserved pool, rollback to previous model variant) and include contact points.
[08:16] Dana: thanks, that helps.
[08:18] [08:18] Closing notes: agreed to reconvene after results; tentative deep-dive scheduled if issues remain.

End of transcript.

References/links mentioned: shared sheet (link redwood/polarwave/pilot-results), pricing delta spreadsheet (to be sent), SOC2 & data residency notes (to be attached).

Audio quality/notes: transcription had some mislabels around the runtime patch ("goroutine" got transcribed once as "goroutine" correctly but other times as "go routine") and occasional mis-typed product names (Redwood Dedicated sometimes read as "Redwood Dedicate").
